header.name: On the making of anthropological objects
header.description:
What is it that anthropologists do? A trivial, rather disappointing answer, is that anthropologists are engaged in the creation of anthropological objects, by talking, writing, and by "doing research". This course seeks to examine how anthropological objects are made, through a careful examination of a series of case studies and through critical texts written by anthropologists on their practices of making knowledge. Although located within the intellectual history of anthropology, the course may be of value to students in allied disciplines, with an interest in problems of philosophy of knowledge. This is an advanced class and may be best suited for students already engaged in research projects. The class will be conducted as a discussion-led symposium centered around 1 or 2 scholarly texts, which are to be read before class. Attendence to the classes is mandatory for success in this course.
The course begins with two contrasting anthropological works, one recent (on online poker), the other, an eighty year old classic of the discipline (on the social and political structure of an African "tribe"). Despite the obvious contrast in their objects of analysis, both these texts are "anthropologies". This course is motivated by the hypothesis that how or why something becomes an object of analytical interest for anthropology, is not at all obvious at first glance. By the end of the course, students setting out to constitute their own research problems, will be able to draw on these critical tools to examine the conditions that make possible the anthropologization of their own objects of interest.
